content: Cholera is an acute diarrheal illness caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. In severe cases, it can lead to rapid dehydration and death. Effective management of cholera requires prompt diagnosis and rehydration therapy, either through oral rehydration salts or intravenous fluids. This review evaluates the additional benefits of using antimicrobial drugs in the treatment of cholera. Antimicrobial therapy significantly reduces the duration of diarrhea by approximately 36.77 hours (about a day and a half) compared to placebo or no treatment. This finding is based on moderate-quality evidence from 19 trials involving 1013 participants. Additionally, antimicrobial treatment decreases the total stool volume by 50%, as shown by a ratio of means (ROM) of 0.5 (95% CI 0.45 to 0.56) from 18 trials with 1042 participants. The need for rehydration fluids is also reduced by 40% (ROM 0.60, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.68) based on data from 11 trials with 1201 participants. Furthermore, the duration of fecal excretion of Vibrio cholerae is shortened by nearly three days (mean difference of 2.74 days, 95% CI -3.07 to -2.40) according to 12 trials with 740 participants. These benefits were observed in patients with both severe and mixed levels of dehydration. The magnitude of these benefits varied across studies, likely due to differences in the antibiotics used, trial methodologies (such as the effectiveness of randomization), and the timing of outcome assessments. When comparing different antibiotics directly, no significant differences were found in diarrhea duration or stool volume between tetracycline and doxycycline (three trials, 230 participants, very low-quality evidence) or between tetracycline and ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin (three trials, 259 participants, moderate-quality evidence). However, indirect comparisons suggest that tetracycline may provide greater benefits than doxycycline, norfloxacin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for the primary outcomes of the review. Single-dose azithromycin was found to reduce the duration of diarrhea by over a day compared to ciprofloxacin (mean difference of -32.43 hours, 95% CI -62.90 to -1.95, two trials, 375 participants, moderate-quality evidence) and by approximately half a day compared to erythromycin (mean difference of -12.05 hours, 95% CI -22.02 to -2.08, two trials, 179 participants, moderate-quality evidence). However, azithromycin was not directly compared with tetracycline in the included studies. In conclusion, the use of antimicrobial drugs in the treatment of cholera leads to significant improvements in both clinical and microbiological outcomes. These benefits are observed in patients with severe as well as non-severe illness. Among the antibiotics studied, azithromycin and tetracycline may offer some advantages over other agents.
